chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shummun from Abdullah ibn al-Rahman from Mis'ma ibn al-Malik from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

That the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to rule regarding the Zindiq when two reputable, just men testified against him and a thousand testified for his acquittal; the testimony of the two men was accepted and the testimony of the thousand was invalidated because it is a concealed religion.

key_terms.الزِّنْدِيق: Zindiq (a person of a concealed religion, typically Zoroastrian or dualist)
key_terms.مَرْضِيَّانِ عَدْلَانِ: Two reputable and just men (experts in the matter)

ai.seo_question: How does Shia jurisprudence handle conflicting testimony between experts and the general public in cases of hidden religion?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the jurisprudential distinction between 'Zindiq' (hidden dualist) and 'Zoroastrian' (manifest pagan) by ruling that two just witnesses suffice for conviction, overriding a thousand witnesses for acquittal. This principle, rooted in the concept of *din makum* (concealed religion), highlights that the general public (*al-alf*) lacks the specialized knowledge to discern the subtle doctrinal deviations of a Zindiq, whereas the two experts (*al-rajulayn*) possess the requisite insight. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the epistemic authority of the knowledgeable over the multitude in matters of hidden religious identity.
